waterSolubility: As arsenate H₃AsO₄: ~16.7 g/L at 20 °C; arsenite H₃AsO₃: ~20 g/L
environmentalPersistence: Very high — does not degrade; arsenic cycles between oxidation states but persists indefinitely

morphologicalEffects.heightSuppression: Strong — arsenate competes with phosphate in energy metabolism
morphologicalEffects.wilting: Moderate-strong — water uptake impaired by root damage
morphologicalEffects.chlorosis: Strong — chloroplast damage and nutrient disruption
morphologicalEffects.necrosis: Strong — root tip necrosis; brown patches on leaves
morphologicalEffects.pigmentation: Mild to moderate — some anthocyanin induction
morphologicalEffects.rootGrowth: Severely inhibited — arsenate entry via phosphate transporters causes direct root toxicity

physiologyEffects.nutrientTransport: Strongly disrupted — arsenate mimics phosphate, disrupts ATP synthesis (arsenate uncouples oxidative phosphorylation)

molecularEffects.oxidativeStress: Strong — arsenite inhibits thiol-containing enzymes; arsenate uncouples ATP synthesis
defenseProteins: phytochelatins (highest induction of all heavy metals)

microbiomeEffects.fungalEffect: Mycorrhizal fungi disrupted; As-resistant strains may persist

temporalDynamics.recoveryTime: None — arsenic accumulates and is not metabolized in most plants

visualSimulation.colorChanges: Green → yellow-green (chlorosis) → brown patches; mild purple tint from anthocyanin
visualSimulation.damageSpread: Upward from roots through vascular tissue
visualSimulation.damagePattern: Patchy brown necrosis on chlorotic background
visualSimulation.heatmapGlow: Strong — As-phytochelatin complex gives distinctive dual peak; strongest of heavy metals on phytochelatin axis
visualSimulation.microbiomeParticles: Sparse; high pathogen fraction; resistome particles elevated

synergies.synergyNote: Arsenic + cadmium is an especially dangerous combination found in rice paddies — both deplete phytochelatins and GSH simultaneously via different mechanisms
synergies.antagonismNote: High phosphate reduces arsenate uptake by competing at phosphate transporter sites

educationalContext.realWorldSources: Contaminated groundwater (Bangladesh, West Bengal — affecting 100M+ people), pesticide legacy contamination, copper smelting, pressure-treated wood (pre-2004)
educationalContext.agriculturalUse: Legacy use as pesticide and herbicide; now banned; contaminates rice through contaminated irrigation water
educationalContext.humanToxicity: Extremely high — IARC Group 1 carcinogen; causes skin, bladder, lung cancer; endemic poisoning in South Asia
educationalContext.climateLink: Climate-driven drought concentrates arsenic in groundwater; flooding mobilizes arsenic from sediments into agricultural soils
educationalContext.indoorOutdoor: Primarily outdoor/water; indoor via contaminated well water in affected regions
educationalContext.whyStudentsCare: The Bangladesh arsenic crisis is one of the largest mass poisonings in human history — drinking water from millions of wells. Rice contamination directly connects to global food security.
educationalContext.realWorldIssue: Groundwater contamination, rice food safety, global health crisis, pressure-treated wood legacy

sources: Meharg AA, Hartley-Whitaker J (2002). Arsenic uptake and metabolism in arsenic resistant and nonresistant plant species. New Phytologist, 154(1), 29–43.
Zhao FJ, et al. (2009). Arsenic as a food chain contaminant: mechanisms of plant uptake and metabolism. Plant and Soil, 325, 1–21.
Finnegan PM, Chen W (2012). Arsenic toxicity: the effects on plant metabolism. Frontiers in Physiology, 3, 182.
